docs.text: GAWP: Germline Analysis with Pandas GAWP is a rewrite and extension of the original Germline Analysis Pipeline (GAP) from the Libuda Lab at the University of Oregon. 1 Our main goal for developing a new script was that we wanted a version that was written in Python and that allowed users to run the code either from the command line or a Jupyter notebook. We also wanted to make it easier for users to adapt the script for new projects. The result is a new organization based on plugins . GAWP has a set of independent modules that perform individual steps of the analysis pipeline. Before running GAWP, users create a configuration file that tells the system the plugins to use and thus which steps to run. The configuration file specifies the sheets from the Imaris output that have the data to use, which columns on those sheets have the relevant data, and various other parameters. The end result is that no settings are "hard wired" into the code -- everything is defined in the configuration file. This should make it easier for new users in the future to run the code on their own data sets (and potentially make it easier to adapt to new data formats from different versions of Imaris). Road Map The sidebar to the left shows the major sections of the documentation. Installation explains how to install GAWP using pip (Python's package installer) There are Tutorials for running GAWP from the command line or in a Jupyter notebook Overview describes how to configure a notebook or script and how to use plugins Plugin Reference has a detailed description of each plugin, along with a complete list of all the options Developer has documentation for people who want to dig in to the Python code Toraason, Erik, Victoria L. Adler, Nicole A. Kurhanewicz, et al. “Automated and Customizable Quantitative Image Analysis of Whole Caenorhabditis Elegans Germlines.” Genetics 217, no. 3 (2021): iyab010. https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyab010. ↩

docs.text: Configuring Plugins At the beginning of each session, either in one of the first few code cells in a notebook or when initializing a command line script, GAWP will read a configuration that specifies which plugins to use. TOML Configurations are written in a simple language named TOML . A configuration is divided into sections . A section begins with a header that has the section name enclosed in brackets. Below that are the specifications, which look like Python assignment statements: an option name, an equal sign, and the value for that option. Values can be integers, strings, or lists. In a GAWP configuration section headers are plugin names . to include a plugin in your workflow, add a section with that name to your configuration some plugins have required settings, and these need to be included in that section other settings are optional; if you leave them out GAWP will use the default value for that setting. An important point to remember: if you want to use a plugin it must appear in the configuration . You might be happy to use the default value for all the options, in which case there will be no settings in that section, but you still need to include the section header. Here is a simple example of a GAWP configuration written in TOML. This workflow will use Geometry and both of its submodules, Foci and Measurements, to linearize a germline. [geometry] sheet_name = 'Position' category_column = 'Category' x_coord = 'Position X' y_coord = 'Position Y' [geometry.foci] index = ['Surpass Object','ID'] [geometry.measurements] The geometry section tells GAWP which sheet has position data and which columns on that sheet have the coordinates of foci and other objects. The geometry.foci and geometry.measurements sections tell GAWP to install these plugins and use the default settings for Measurements. Configuring Join and Group Plugins Because a project might want to copy or group data from several different sheets the syntax for the section header is slightly different and there can be multiple sections in the configuration. To add a Join or Group plugin to a project, write the word join or group , a period, and then a name. The name of the sheet and the name of the column on that sheet must be specified. By default the Join and Group plugins expect to see the same ID columns that were used for Geometry, but it they are different the names to use instead can be specified as well. In this example a project wants to copy volume and sphericity data to the output. [join.volume] sheet = 'Volume' column = 'Volume' [join.sphericity] sheet = 'Sphericity' column = 'Sphericity' Configuration Cells in Jupyter Notebooks To run GAWP from a Jupyter notebook: import the GAWP modules that implement the plugins create a piece of text that has the TOML specification pass that specification to the GAWP function that installs the plugins Here are some examples from a workflow that will use the Geometry plugin. Imports The first statement imports the GAWP function that installs plugins. Below that are statements that import the plugins themselves. from gawp.config import initialize_config from gawp.geometry import Geometry from gawp.foci import Foci ... TOML String This statement defines a string named GAWP_CONFIG using Python's "triple-quoted string" syntax, which lets us create strings that span multiple lines: GAWP_CONFIG = ''' [geometry] sheet_name = 'Position' category_column = 'Category' x_coord = 'Position X' y_coord = 'Position Y' [geometry.foci] category = 'Surface' index = ['Surpass Object','ID'] ''' Install the Plugins Finally we pass GAWP_CONFIG to initialize_config to install the plugins: initialize_config(text=GAWP_CONFIG) Configuration Files for the Command Line Script Python scripts read configurations from files. TOML files are plain text files that can be created with any text editor. The filename extension is usually .toml . gawp , the command line application installed by pip, looks for a file named gawp.toml in the directory where the script is started. To tell it to read a different file, include the --config option on the command line, for example: $ gawp --config rad51.toml run Summary: Define Plugins Using TOML Call initialize_config at the beginning of a notebook or script. Pass it a piece of text or the name of a file. The spec should have a section for each plugin to use in the workflow.

docs.text: Geometry All of the "heavy lifting" of the linearization pipeline is done in the Geometry module. The data used by this module is typically on a sheet named "Positions", such as this one from an example data set: There are three different groupings in this sheet. The first set of rows (highlighted in red) have "Spot" in the Category column. The next group (highlighted in blue) has "Surface" in the Category column, and the last group (highlighted in green) has "MeasurementPoint". For this project we want the plugin to ignore the spots, make a data point for each surface, and combine adjacent measurement points into line segments. Plugin Configurations The attributes that can be assigned in the geometry section of the configuration are listed in this table: Attribute Default Note sheet_name Position category_column Category name of column with category values x_coord Position X x_coord Position Y The attributes that can be specified in geometry.foci : Attribute Default Note category 'Surface' index ['Surpass Object','ID'] columns are concatenated to form data point IDs The attributes that can be specified in geometry.measurements : Attribute Default Note category 'MeasurementPoint' index Name Note: The geometry.foci and geometry.measurements sections "inherit" all of the attributes listed in the geometry section shown above. If a project has foci or measurements on different sheets or attributes in different columns those attributes can be overridden in these sections. Example The configuration section for the example uses all of the default values, so it only has to name the plugins: [geometry] [geometry.foci] [geometry.measurements] Here are the resulting frames after the data is read from the spreadsheet: Linearization Algorithm The first step in the linearization algorithm is to compute all possible distances. We can start this process by making a table that has every combination of data point and line segment using an operation called the "cross product". The next steps are: compute the distances and add them to the cross product frame. group the rows by IDs find the minimum distance in each group The final result is a data frame that has one row for each nucleus. In that row are the name of the nearest line segment, the point where a line from the nucleus intersects the line segment, and the total length of a path from the first measurement point up to the intersection point. API The Geometry plugin is accessed via the Plugin Manager . Attributes plugins.geometry A reference to the Geometry plugin. plugins.geometry.foci A reference to the Foci plugin. plugins.geometry.measurements A reference to the Measurements plugin. plugins.geometry.position_frame A Pandas DataFrame with the locations of the foci read from the Imaris spreadsheeet. The frame has the following columns: index: a unique ID formed by concatenating the columns defined in the id_cols settings in the configuration point : a GeoPandas POINT object with the coordinates of the data point. plugins.geometry.measurement_frame A Pandas DataFrame the locations of the measurement points read from the Imaris spreadsheeet. The frame has the following columns: index: the name of the measurement point point : a GeoPandas POINT object with the coordinates of the measurement point. plugins.geometry.segment_frame A Pandas DataFrame with descriptions of line segments formed by connecting adjacent measurement points. The frame has the following columns: index: the name of the line segment, formed by concatenating two measurement point IDs head : the point at the start of the segment tail : the point at the end of the segment segment : a GeoPandas LINESTRING object with the head and tail of the segment orientation : a string (NW, NE, SE, SW) intended to be used by visualizaation algorithms A and C : parameters of the linear equation of the segment length : the length of the segment pathlen : the sum of distances from the start of the first segment to the start of this segment plugins.geometry.linearized_frame A Pandas DataFrame with the output of the linearization algorithm. The frame has the following columns: index: the name of a data point seg_name : the ID of the line segment closest to the point point : the coordinates of the data point head : the of the closest line segment tail : the tail of the closest line segment distance : the distance from the data point to the line segment loc : the point on the segment that is closest to the data point orientation : a string (NW, NE, SE, SW) intended to be used by visualizaation algorithms pathlen : the sum of distances from the start of the first segment to the start of the segments closest to the point pathseg : the distance from the start of the segment to the location where a line from the data point intersects the segment pathloc : the normalized distance from the start of the first segment to the location where the data point intersects the segment Methods plugins.geometry.apply(xls_file) Read the positions of foci and measurments from an open XLS file. plugins.geometry.linearize() Execute the linearization algorithm. If a Measurement plugin is configured the output is a frame that has the closest line segment to each data point, otherwise the output is just a referencee to the positions of the points.

docs.text: Group Counting Spots The Group stage summarizes the data in one of the sheets to produce counts. The process is best explained using a sheet from one of the example data sets. A sheet named "Intensity Max Ch=4 Img=1" has a table that connects spots to surfaces. This is what the sheet looks like in Excel: There are two parts to the table. The upper part has the word "Surface" in the Category column, and the lower part (shaded in green) has "Spot" in that column. The essential thing to know about this table is that unlike most other sheets, the leftmost column, labeled "Intensity Max", does not actually contain intensity values. Those numbers are IDs. For the surface rows IDs are numbers ranging from 1 to 53, which is the number of surfaces in the data set. For the spots, the number in the left column is the ID of the surface that (according to Imaris) the spot is closest to. Most spots have a 0 in this column, which means the spot is not associated with any surface. But you can see at the bottom of the figure, in row 5283, there is a 10 in the leftmost column, which means this spot is closest to surface number 10. Other spots below that have 9, 10, or 11 in the leftmost column, meaning they are close to surfaces with those IDs. Algorithm The Group stage gets its name from groupby , another concept borrowed from relational databases and widely used in Pandas and other data science libraries. The main steps in this plugin are: Split the sheet into two parts and make two data frames, one for surfaces and one for spots Group the spots according to their IDs, and count the number of rows in each group; note that the name of each group is the ID of one of the surfaces Append the counts to the end of the surfaces frame using a join operation that connects counts to surfaces using the ID column Here is what the group operation looks like: Note that the first row is the count of the number of spots that have 0 in the "Intensity Max" column. This count is ignored when the counts are joined with the surfaces. The result of that join is shown below. The yellow shading highlights the fact that the join is using the column named "Intensity Max" and that this column appears in both the spots and surfaces frames. Plugin Configuration The configuration section that adds a Group plugin should have a name consisting of the word "group", a period, and a name. Within each section define the attributes to use for that plugin: Attribute Default Note sheet (required) name of the sheet with data to join column (required) column that contains the data to copy category_column '' column for filtering rows category '' value for filtering rows group (required) the value for rows to group by aggregation_function count aggregation_name (required) name for the output column index '' names of columns for creating IDs If the category_column , category , or index attributes are left out they are copied from the Geometry plugin. Example This is the configuration section that was used for the example data shown above: [group.intensity] sheet = 'Intensity Max Ch=4 Img=1' category_column = 'Category' category = 'Surface' group = 'Spot' column = 'Intensity Max' aggregation_function = 'count' aggregation_name = 'RAD51' API The Group plugins are accessed via the Plugin Manager . plugins.group A reference to the top level Group plugin, which maintains a list of objects, one for each group to create. plugins.group.sheets A list of GroupSheet objects, each of which has specifications for grouping one column. plugins.join.grouped_frame A Pandas DataFrame created by the apply method. It has one column for each group created. Methods plugins.group.apply() Iterates over all sheets, extracting the data, forming groups, and saving them in the output frame.

docs.text: Use pip to Install GAWP GAWP is a standard Python package that can be installed using pip . Reduce the Noise Level When pip installs GAWP it is most likely going to add a lot of new libraries to your system. Before you install you might want to consider creating a virtual environment. See Do You Need a Virtual Environment? below. Simply open a new terminal window and type this shell command: $ pip install git+https://github.com/conery/gawp.git If all the installation steps succeed you will have a new command line application named gawp . You can run it with the --help option to make sure everything was installed correctly: $ gawp --help usage: gawp [-h] [--log X] [--preview] [--config F] {run,review,status} ... You will also have a new module that you can import into your notebooks or Python scripts. For example, the IO plugin has a function that reads a sheet from an XLS file and converts it into a Pandas dataframe. To use this function your code could include this line: from gawp.io import open_spreadsheet Do You Need a Virtual Environment? When pip installs GAWP it will check to make sure all of the libraries it depends on are also installed. Mostly these are well-known data science libraries like Pandas that you probably already have. But there are several that you might not have: Shapely, a geography library we use for computing distances between points and line segments GeoPandas, a library that allows us to put Shapely objects in Pandas dataframes Rich, an all-around useful library for creating interfaces for command line applications We strongly recommend installing GAWP in its own virtual environment . That will prevent several potential problems. For example, if you have an older version of Pandas on your system, pip will want to upgrade it, and that could break some other programs you have that depend on the older version. If you have recent versions of Pandas and Numpy and are not concerned with installing these new libraries (they're not likely to conflict with any libraries you have already) then go ahead and type the pip command to install GAWP. But if you're ready to take control of your Python data science environments the best approach is to use a package named pyenv and a companion plugin named pyenv-virtualenv . After you create a clean new environment activate it and then type the pip command to install GAWP. pip will do the rest by installing Pandas and the other modules used by GAWP.
docs.title: Use pip to Install GAWP

docs.text: IO GAWP's io module defines the IO plugin and several functions that can be called from notebooks that do not need to use the plugin itself. Plugin Configuration The section name to use when configuring the IO plugin is [io] . The configuration option are listed in the table below. Option Default Description spreadsheets '' The name(s) of Imaris spreadsheets to analyze output_dir '' Directory for output files output_name '' A pattern to use for output files log '' The name of a file for log messages spreadsheets The value of the spreadsheets option can be a single file name or a name pattern containing wildcards. Name patterns have the same syntax used in shell commands, i.e. they can use question marks and asterisks as wild cards. If the name is a pattern it is expanded and the script will process all of the files that match the pattern. File names are relative to the directory where the script is run. For example, the pattern "../data/*" means "all files in a folder named data in the directory above the current working directory." output_dir This is the name of a directory where output files will be written. As with spreadsheet names, the name is relative to the current directory. output_name This parameter is a pattern to use for output files. When writing a pattern, the string "{fn}" will be replaced by the name of the current input file. For example, suppose a directory named data has three spreadsheets named a.xls , b.xls , and c.xls . The configuration would have "data/*" for spreadsheets . The pattern "linear_{fn}" would tell GAWP to write the outputs to linear_a.xls m linear_b.xls , and linear.c.xls . log Not implemented yet. Example Ths configuration tells GAWP to process every spreadsheet (a file ending with .xlsx ) in a directory named data . The script will create a directory named output in the folder where the script is run, and ouput files will have the same name as input files but with the word "linearized" added to the front of the name. [io] spreadsheets = 'data/*.xlsx' output_dir = './output' output_name = 'linearized_{fn.stem}' open_spreadsheet Call this function to open an Excel spreadsheet. There is only one parameter, the name of the file to open. The value returned is an ExcelFile object that can be passed to fetch_sheet to read data from the spreadsheet. The function works with either older style .xls files or the newer .xlsx format. fetch_sheet Call fetch_sheet to read a sheet of data from an Excel file. The data will be return as a Pandas DataFrame object. The first argument passed in the call must be an ExcelFile object created by calling open_spreadsheet . The second must be the name of the sheet to read the data from. There are two additional arguments that can be passed: id_cols is a list of one or more column names. If no column names are passed the index will be the integers starting from 0 (the default RangeIndex in Pandas). If column names are passed, the function will concatenate the values in those columns to create the index. filter_cols will select a subset of the rows from the sheet. Pass a list of two items: the name of a column and a value to filter by. The output frame will contain only the rows where this value is found in the column. Example

docs.text: Join The Join stage copies data without modifying it and saves it in a table that can be combined with results from other plugins. The configuration file specifies which sheets have the data and which columns on those sheets to copy. The name "join" comes from relational databases, where the concept originated. It is now standard terminology in R, Pandas, and other data science libraries that work with tabular data. The tables created by the Join plugin have names for data points that are compatible with the names assigned by other plugins. Typically this is a name formed by combining the Category and ID columns in each table. A join operation makes sure rows with matching IDs are aligned with each other. Plugin Configuration The configuration section that adds a Join plugin should have a name consisting of the word "join", a period, and a name. Within each section define the attributes to use for that plugin: Attribute Default Note sheet (required) name of the sheet with data to join column (required) column that contains the data to copy category_column '' column for filtering rows category '' value for filtering rows index '' names of columns for creating IDs The first two attributes are required. If the remaining attributes are left out they are copied from the Geometry plugin. Example This configuration copies data from the Volume and Sphericity sheets, using the default column names for IDs. [join.volume] sheet = 'Volume' column = 'Volume' [join.sphericity] sheet = 'Sphericity' column = 'Sphericity' Here is the frame produced by the stage, with columns ready to be included in the final output: API The Join plugins are accessed via the Plugin Manager . Attributes plugins.join A reference to the top level Join plugin, which maintains a list of objects, one for each column to copy. plugins.join.sheets A list of JoinSheet objects, each of which has specifications for copying one column. plugins.join.combined_frame A Pandas DataFrame created by the apply method. It has one column for each sheet copied. Methods plugins.join.apply() Iterates over all sheets, extracting the data and saving it in the output frame.
docs.title: Join

The configuration file specifies which sheets have the data and which columns on those sheets to copy. The name "join" comes from relational databases, where the concept originated. It is now standard terminology in R, Pandas, and other data science libraries that work with tabular data. The tables created by the Join plugin have names for data points that are compatible with the names assigned by other plugins. Typically this is a name formed by combining the Category and ID columns in each table. A join operation makes sure rows with matching IDs are aligned with each other.

docs.text: The configuration section that adds a Join plugin should have a name consisting of the word "join", a period, and a name. Within each section define the attributes to use for that plugin: Attribute Default Note sheet (required) name of the sheet with data to join column (required) column that contains the data to copy category_column '' column for filtering rows category '' value for filtering rows index '' names of columns for creating IDs The first two attributes are required. If the remaining attributes are left out they are copied from the Geometry plugin.

docs.text: Plugin Manager The Plugin Manager is a module that keeps track of which plugins have been installed for an application. GAWP defines a global variable named plugins that can be accessed by all of the modules in GAWP and by applications. As the initialize_config function creates plugins they are registered with the plugin manager, where they become accessible as attributes of the plugins object. All of the attributes are initially set to None . An application can check to see if a plugin was installed by testing the value of an attribute, e.g. if plugins.join is not None: # do something with joins Attribute Plugin Notes plugins.io IO required by command line applications plugins.geometry Geometry plugins.geometry.foci Foci plugins.geometry.measurements Measurements plugins.join Join a list of JoinSheet objects plugins.group Group a list of GroupSheet objects plugins.stages Stages

docs.text: Using Plugins in An Application When the initialize_config function creates the plugins requested in a configuration file it registers them with a module called the plugin manager . Applications use the manager to figure out which plugins are installed, to run the plugins, and to access their outputs when they have finished. The module is named plugins . To use it, import it into your application: from gawp.plugin import plugins Accessing Plugins After the module is imported you can refer to the plugins by name, e.g. plugins.geometry or plugins.stages . These names are all defined when GAWP is first imported, but they are all set to None . After you call initialize_config the names are updated and will be references to the objects that implement the stage. In this example, a notebook defines a workflow that only has the three geometry plugins, so plugins.stages is still None after the setup. Running Plugins To execute the part of the workflow defined by a plugin call one or more methods defined in the plugin's module. For example, the Geometry plugin has a method named apply . It reads the positions of the foci and (if Measurements is installed) the positions of the measurement points, saving them in data frames that can be accessed later. The sections below have a brief overview of the plugins and methods that are most likely to be used in a Jupyter notebook. For more details see the complete documentation at Plugin Manager . Geometry plugins.geometry.apply(xls_file) Read the positions of foci and (if configured) measurments from an open XLS file. Saves the results in plugins.geometry.position_frame and plugins.geometry.measurement_frame . plugins.geometry.linearize() Execute the linearization algorithm. Returns a Pandas DataFrame, indexd by data point ID, containing the name of the closest line segment and coordinates of the where a line from the point intersects the segment. The data frame is also saved as plugins.geometry.linearized_frame . Join plugins.join.apply(xls_file) Create a Pandas DataFrame that has one column of output for each sheet specified in the configuration file. The data frame is also saved as plugins.join.combined_frame . Group plugins.group.apply(xls_file) Create a Pandas DataFrame that has one column of output for each sheet specified in the configuration file. The data frame is also saved as plugins.join.grouped_frame . Stages plugins.stages.apply(fn, df) The arguments are the name fn of the spreadsheet fn and a frame df that is indexed by data point ID and has the name of the line segment closest to the point. Look up the stage breaks for the file and create a Pandas DataFrame that has the meiotic stage for each point. The result is also saved as plugins.stages.stage_frame Note: The names of segments are in the frame created by the Geometry plugin, in a column named seg_name . This is how the main loop in the command line application calls stages.apply : plugins.stages.apply(fn, plugins.geometry.linearized_frame[['seg_name']])

docs.text: Define a Workflow with Plugins GAWP is organized as a set of plugin modules that carry out individual steps of the full linearization workflow. Plugin Name Module Name Resonsibilities IO gawp.io Opens spreadsheets, extracts data from sheets Geometry gawp.geometry Computes distances between points and line segments Foci gawp.geometry.foci Reads positions of foci Measurements gawp.geometry.measurements Reads measurement points, uses them to create line segments Join gawp.join Copies data from Volume, Sphericity, and other sheets Group gawp.group Summarizes Intensity data to create counts Stages gawp.stages Assigns meiotic stage names to foci Each application decides which of these plugins to install. A minimal workflow might use only Geometry, Foci, and Join in order to create a table that has positions of foci and their attributes, skipping the linearization step. At the other extreme, a project can use all of the plugins to implement the full linearization pipeline. The sections below have short descriptions of each plugin. Complete details are in the Plugins section (linked in the menu bar on the left). IO Jupyter notebooks and command line applications all need to open XLS files exported from Imaris, read data from different sheets inside those spreadsheets, and save results. But notebooks and scripts have different requirements. Someone using a notebook can focus in a single data set, often to explore how different steps of the workflow apply to that data. They can tell GAWP which spreadsheet they want to open and tell it exactly what they want it to do with that notebook. The results of different steps are displayed in the notebook, and that may be all the user needs to see -- there is no need to write the results to a file. A user running GAWP from the command line has different goals. They know exactly what the steps are, and they want GAWP to apply those steps to several different spreadsheets, maybe even every spreadsheet in a folder exported by Imaris. They also want the results of running the pipeline saved in a new directory, where output file names are derived from the input file names. They also might want to have GAWP generate a log file so there is a record of what it did. GAWP's io module supports both of these use cases. The plugin named IO is used by command line applications to manage interactions with multiple spreadsheets. The module also defines standalone functions , such as parse_spreadsheet , that can be called from notebooks. Not surprisingly, the plugin calls the standalone functions -- it's goal is to automate the workflow by calling these functions automatically for every spreadsheet the user wants to analyze. Geometry, Foci, and Measurements The locations of foci, measurements, and other items are typically saved on the "Positions" sheet of spreadsheets exported by Imaris. GAWP's Geometry plugin reads and organizes this data. To use some terminology from object-oriented programming, Geometry is the base class, and Foci and Measurements are derived classes. The Geometry plugin has operations common to all items on the "Positions" sheet: the name of the sheet, the name of the column used to distinguish foci from the other items, and the $x$ and $y$ locations of the data. Foci and Measurements have operations specific to those types of data: foci are saved an initial data frame that will be used as input to the linearization algorithm measurement points are saved in a data frame, and then another frame, holding line segments, is built by connecting adjacent measurements If a project works with foci the configuruation needs to include both the Geometry and Foci plugins. If Measurements plugin is included in the configuration the linearization algorithm will be called. The final result computed by the Geometry plugins will be a data frame that is indexed by the names of foci and with columns for the $x$ and $y$ locations and other attributes of the foci. As the remaining plugins are executed they will columns to the table. Join If an Imaris spreadhseet has additional data besides positions of foci this other data can be copied to the output with a Join plugin. A project might want to copy several different types of data, which means the configuration can have several different join sections. A key point is the other sheets must have the same columns used to create IDs for the foci. The Join plugin will read another sheet, find the column requested in the configuration, and adds it to the output frame. Group The Group plugin is similar to Join, but it has a twist. After reading the data from the specified sheet, the rows are grouped and then an "aggregation function" is applied to each group. The result of the aggregation is added as a new column in the output frame. Stages If a project has a spreadsheet that defines meiotic stages the Stages plugin will use that spreadsheet to add a new column to the output frame.
docs.title: Define a Workflow with Plugins

docs.text: Stages The data for adding transitions between meiotic stages is kept in a separate spreadsheet from the data exported by Imaris. This extra spreadsheet has one row for every data set. The leftmost column has the names of Imaris spreadsheets. Next to that are columns for transitions between stages and additional notes. The Stages plugin creates a new column to add to the final output. For each data point the plugin uses the ID of the closest line segment (now saved in the seg_name column of the linearized data frame) to assign the meiotic stage according to the measurement points in the stage table. Plugin Configuration The attributes that can be assigned in the stages section of the configuration are listed in this table: Attribute Default Note file (required) name of the XLS file with stage transitions index 'GonadID' the name of the column with file names filter_column 'Stitched?' name of a column to filter rows filter 'TRUE' use rows that have this value in the filter column stage_columns ['TZ_start','TZ_end','Pachy_end'] the names of the columns with stage transitions stage_names ['PMT', 'TZ', 'PACH' the names to use in the output Example Here is part of the output for the example data: The plugin looked in columns named TZ_start , TZ_end , and Pachy_end to find the transitions. For example, since TZ_start is G for this data set, all rows in the linearized frame that have a segment that starts before G are assigned PMT (the output name for this stage). All rows that have segments between G and L are assigned TZ , and so on. Note: The plugin does not make any assumptions about names of stages or how many stages there are. As long as the number of column names matches the number of stage names the names will be assigned. API The Stages plugin is accessed via the Plugin Manager . Attributes plugins.stages A reference to the Stages plugin. plugins.stages.boundaries A Pandas DataFrame based on the contents of the stage transitions spreadsheet, containing one row per data set. plugins.stages.stage_frame A Pandas DataFrame created by the apply method. It will have the same number of rows and same index as the segments frame passed to apply , and one column with assigned stage names. Methods plugins.stages.read_stage_boundaries() Opens the XLS file containing stage transitions (using the file name from the configuration), saves the contents as a Pandas DataFrame. plugins.group.apply(fn, segments) Assign meiotic stage names to each data point. fn is the name of a data set (the name of the file used to find stage names in the stage transitions table). segments is a frame with segment names, indexed by data point ID. docs.text: Run GAWP from the Command Line The gawp script installed by Python is designed for "batch processing" of several Imaris outputs. In this tutorial we'll start out with a minimal configuration file and show how to execute the workflow it defines. Then we'll add more plugins to illustrate additional features of the command line application. Sample Data and Project Directory An archive with sample data can be downloaded from GitHub. To start this tutorial download and unzip the folder. You should end up with a new folder named gawp_demo with the following items: gawp_demo ├── data # a folder for the sample notebooks │ ├── herm_5.xlsx # three Imaris spreadsheets with sample data │ ├── herm_7.xlsx │ └── herm_9.xlsx ├── gawp.toml # project configuration file Throughout the rest of the tutorial we'll assume you will be running gawp from this folder.
docs.title: Introduction

docs.text: The gawp script installed by Python is designed for "batch processing" of several Imaris outputs. In this tutorial we'll start out with a minimal configuration file and show how to execute the workflow it defines. Then we'll add more plugins to illustrate additional features of the command line application.
docs.title: Run GAWP from the Command Line

docs.text: The gawp Command Like most shell commands we run gawp by typing its name followed by various options and arguments. Type this to see the "usage" message: $ gawp --help usage: gawp [-h] [--log X] {run,review,status} ... options: -h, --help show this help message and exit --log X ... The output shows that gawp has subcommands named run , review , and status . We'll focus on the first one in this tutorial since it's the command that runs a workflow. So now we can see that to run gawp , we type gawp , then the name of the subcommand, and then any options or arguments for that subcommand. To see the full list of options for the run subcommand type this: $ gawp run --help usage: gawp run [-h] [--config F] [--file F [F ...]] [--output D] [--preview] [--force] ... Two options to learn first are --file , and --preview . --file is the name of the input file (Imaris spreadsheet) that has the data to analyze --preview tells the script to print the first few lines of the output on terminal (instead of saving the output in a file) We'll introduce the remaining options as we progress through the tutorial. Go ahead and type the command shown below. It will run the sample workflow on a single spreadsheet named herm_5.xlsx : $ gawp run --preview --file data/herm_5.xlsx ... Preview for herm_5: point pdk.123 POINT (19.469 128.836) pdk.174 POINT (1.258 138.006) pdk.293 POINT (21.258 112.538) ... Reduce the Noise Level gawp printed a lot of messages to the terminal along with that output. If you want to turn off these messages type --log quiet after gawp and before run : $ gawp --log quiet run --preview ... At the other extreme, if you want more information, use --log debug . Debug messages are mainly for developers but they might have some useful information if gawp is not doing what you expect it to. Important: if you use --log notice where it goes on the command line, after gawp but before run .

docs.text: The Configuration File GAWP configurations use a file format named TOML. TOML files are plain text and can be opened with any text editor. Go ahead and open gawp.toml now. Our intial configuration file has just one line: [geometry.foci] That line is a section header . It has the name of a plugin enclosed in square brackets. The fact that there is only one plugin name in this configuration file means gawp will execute only this one step when we run it. This plugin fetches the locations of foci from a Position sheet; a workflow that consists of just this step will simply read the positions and write them to the output file. Section Names Define Plugins The important message to take away from this part of the tutorial is that gawp will run only the plugins that appear as section headers in the configuration file. Let's add another step to the workflow. Add the following lines: [geometry.measurements] sheet_name = 'Position' category_column = 'Category' category = 'MeasurementPoint' The lines below the section heading specify options for the plugin. Options are lines that look like Python assignment statements: they have a setting name, an equal sign, and a value. In this example we're telling the Measurements plugin that measurements are found on a sheet named Position, and to look in the Category column for rows that have "MeasurementPoint" in that column. The upated workflow has two steps: read the foci and read the measurement points. When measurement points are included gawp will make line segments from the points and run the linearization algorithm to map foci to line segments. Save the modified configuration and run the script again: $ gawp --log quiet run --preview --file data/herm_5.xlsx Preview for herm_5: seg_name point head tail distance ... uid pdk.123 AB POINT (19.469 128.836) POINT (38.501 141.542) POINT (39.457 120.56) 19.590598 ... pdk.174 AB POINT (1.258 138.006) POINT (38.501 141.542) POINT (39.457 120.56) 37.365346 ... ... The column named point was there in the previous output. In the new output the Measurement plugin added seg_name and all the other columns that are the result of mapping the points to line segments. Default Settings You probably noticed the original configuration file did not include options for the [geometry.foci] section. That plugin also has several options, but since the configuration file did not include them the plugin used the default values. All of the available plugins are shown in the Plugins section in the sidebar, and a complete list of options and their default values are included in the descriptions of the plugins.
docs.title: Configuration File

docs.text: Input Files The --file argument on the command line can contain wildcards. This example tells gawp to run the pipeline on all the files in the data directory: $ gawp --log quiet run --preview --file data/* Preview for herm_5: seg_name point head tail distance ... uid pdk.123 AB POINT (19.469 128.836) POINT (38.501 141.542) POINT (39.457 120.56) 19.590598 ... pdk.174 AB POINT (1.258 138.006) POINT (38.501 141.542) POINT (39.457 120.56) 37.365346 ... ... Preview for herm_7: seg_name point head tail distance ... uid pep.217 FG POINT (120.258 57.426) POINT (123.785 59.548) POINT (99.631 51.754) 0.936370 ... pep.263 FG POINT (115.396 57.698) POINT (123.785 59.548) POINT (99.631 51.754) 0.815551 ... ... Preview for herm_9: seg_name point head tail distance ... uid pdk.148 IJ POINT (54.723 37.05) POINT (63.489 49.701) POINT (49.47 41.754) 6.682733 ... pdk.149 IJ POINT (58.296 33.857) POINT (63.489 49.701) POINT (49.47 41.754) 11.222490 ... ... Another way to tell gawp where to find the input files is to add an IO plugin to the configuration file and to define the file names in the spreadsheet option. Open gawp.config with your editor and add this section: [io] spreadsheets = 'data/*.xlsx' Now that the file names are defined in the configuration file we don't need the --file option on the command line. This "minimal" command will get the input file names from gawp.toml and run the pipeline in preview mode: $ gawp run --preview Command Line Takes Precedence If a configuration file defines spreadsheet names in an IO plugin and there is a --file option in the command the name(s) on the command line are used. On a related note, if there is no IO plugin and the command does not have a --file option the script will print an error message since it doesn't know where to find input files.

docs.text: Join The next plugin to add to the workflow is called Join . The goal is to find a column of data from one of the other sheets and append it to the dataframe that will be saved at the end of the workflow. The name "join" comes from the relational database world. When the new column is added, the script can't simply copy and paste the column from the other sheet because the rows might not be in the same order as the foci in the Position sheet. Instead, to make sure the data is aligned properly, the script has to use an item's ID from one sheet and connect it with an item with the same ID in the other sheet. The configuration file has to tell the script how to make a unique identifier for each data point. In the test data, the IDs are made by concatenating strings from the "Surpass Object" and "ID" columns. As an example, here are the first few rows of the Position sheet for the first data file ( herm_5.xslx ): The IDs made by the script become the index values in the data frame. The name of the index is uid (for "unique identifier") and it is displayed in the leftmost column when the frame is printed on the terminal: Preview for herm_5: seg_name point head tail ... uid pdk.123 AB POINT (19.469 128.836) POINT (38.501 141.542) POINT (39.457 120.56) ... pdk.174 AB POINT (1.258 138.006) POINT (38.501 141.542) POINT (39.457 120.56) ... ... Now suppose we want to add the "Volume" column from the sheet of the same name to the output. This is the sheet as its shown in Excel: Note it has the same "Surpass Object" and "ID" columns, but the rows are not in the same order. This sheet is orderd by ID, so rows with smaller numbers in that column are at the top of the sheet. The Position sheet is ordered by Surpass Object, so rows with "pdk" appear first, then rows with "pek", and so on. But if we concatenate the strings to make unique IDs we can match objects in one sheet with objects in the other sheet. Let's add two Join plugins in the workflow, one for volume and one for sphericity. Add these lines to your configuration file: [join.volume] sheet = 'Volume' column = 'Volume' index = ['Surpass Object','ID'] [join.sphericity] sheet = 'Sphericity' column = 'Sphericity' index = ['Surpass Object','ID'] Note how the section names have the word "join" followed by a period and another name. If we just used the word "join" by itself we would have two sections with the same name, but TOML doesn't allow that, so we have to add those qualifiers. In both of these new sections we specify the name of the sheet in the XLS file that has the data we want to copy, the name of the column on that sheet (which just happens to be the same name), and the names of the columns to use when forming the unique identifiers. After you add those sections to your config file and run the script again you'll see the new columns at the end of the output: $ gawp --log quiet run --preview Preview for herm_5: seg_name point ... pathlen pathseg pathloc Volume Sphericity uid pdk.123 AB POINT (19.469 128.836) ... 0.000000 11.826586 0.049429 0.017 0.731 pdk.174 AB POINT (1.258 138.006) ... 0.000000 1.837206 0.007679 0.001 0.561 ... Preview for herm_7: seg_name point ... pathlen pathseg pathloc Volume Sphericity uid pep.217 FG POINT (120.258 57.426) ... 188.943937 4.008221 0.729937 0.000 0.634 pep.263 FG POINT (115.396 57.698) ... 188.943937 8.551765 0.747126 0.000 0.729 ... Preview for herm_9: seg_name point ... pathlen pathseg pathloc Volume Sphericity uid pdk.148 IJ POINT (54.723 37.05) ... 197.050149 13.864763 0.989445 0.013 0.733 pdk.149 IJ POINT (58.296 33.857) ... 197.050149 12.331072 0.982250 0.002 0.671 ...

docs.text: The next plugin to add to the workflow is called Join . The goal is to find a column of data from one of the other sheets and append it to the dataframe that will be saved at the end of the workflow. The name "join" comes from the relational database world. When the new column is added, the script can't simply copy and paste the column from the other sheet because the rows might not be in the same order as the foci in the Position sheet. Instead, to make sure the data is aligned properly, the script has to use an item's ID from one sheet and connect it with an item with the same ID in the other sheet. The configuration file has to tell the script how to make a unique identifier for each data point. In the test data, the IDs are made by concatenating strings from the "Surpass Object" and "ID" columns. As an example, here are the first few rows of the Position sheet for the first data file ( herm_5.xslx ): The IDs made by the script become the index values in the data frame. The name of the index is uid (for "unique identifier") and it is displayed in the leftmost column when the frame is printed on the terminal: Preview for herm_5: seg_name point head tail ... uid pdk.123 AB POINT (19.469 128.836) POINT (38.501 141.542) POINT (39.457 120.56) ... pdk.174 AB POINT (1.258 138.006) POINT (38.501 141.542) POINT (39.457 120.56) ... ... Now suppose we want to add the "Volume" column from the sheet of the same name to the output. This is the sheet as its shown in Excel: Note it has the same "Surpass Object" and "ID" columns, but the rows are not in the same order. This sheet is orderd by ID, so rows with smaller numbers in that column are at the top of the sheet. The Position sheet is ordered by Surpass Object, so rows with "pdk" appear first, then rows with "pek", and so on. But if we concatenate the strings to make unique IDs we can match objects in one sheet with objects in the other sheet. If we just used the word "join" by itself we would have two sections with the same name, but TOML doesn't allow that, so we have to add those qualifiers. In both of these new sections we specify the name of the sheet in the XLS file that has the data we want to copy, the name of the column on that sheet (which just happens to be the same name), and the names of the columns to use when forming the unique identifiers. After you add those sections to your config file and run the script again you'll see the new columns at the end of the output: $ gawp --log quiet run --preview Preview for herm_5: seg_name point ... pathlen pathseg pathloc Volume Sphericity uid pdk.123 AB POINT (19.469 128.836) ... 0.000000 11.826586 0.049429 0.017 0.731 pdk.174 AB POINT (1.258 138.006) ... 0.000000 1.837206 0.007679 0.001 0.561 ... Preview for herm_7: seg_name point ... pathlen pathseg pathloc Volume Sphericity uid pep.217 FG POINT (120.258 57.426) ... 188.943937 4.008221 0.729937 0.000 0.634 pep.263 FG POINT (115.396 57.698) ... 188.943937 8.551765 0.747126 0.000 0.729 ... docs.text: Output Files The steps we've worked through so far in this tutorial follow a process we recommend each time you need to create a new GAWP workflow: start with a minimal configuration run gawp in with the --preview option on one or two data files to make sure you're getting the columns you expect add new stages one at a time and test the results on the same data files In previous sections we assembled a workflow that does the linearization steps and adds columns from other sheets, and configured the workflow to apply these steps to every spreadsheet in a folder. The last step is to save the results to output files. For this, all we need to do is add a couple of new lines to the configuration section for the IO plugin: we need to tell GAWP where to put the output files we also want to tell it how to create the output file names Open your configuration and edit the section labeled [io] so it looks like the code below. You should already have the first line in the section, you want to add the next two. [io] spreadsheets = 'data/herm*.xlsx' output_dir = './output' output_name = 'linearized_{fn.stem}' The output_dir setting tells the script to create a new directory named output in the current folder. The output_name is a pattern that means "the name of the output file should be the word 'linearized' in front of the name of the input file". After you save the updated configuration you're ready to run the script. If you type the same command that you have used in previous steps it will still have the --preview option, so it will look like nothing changed: all the output will be printed on the console. But when you remove the --preview the script will save the output files. We suggest testing the command with a single data file to make sure you're getting the output you expect: $ gawp run --file data/herm_5.xlsx You should now have a new folder named output , and inside that folder a text file named linearized_herm_5.csv : gawp_demo ├── data │ ├── herm_5.xlsx │ ├── herm_7.xlsx │ └── herm_9.xlsx ├── gawp.toml └── output └── linearized_herm_5.csv Safety Switch When you're convinced things are working, run the command again, this time without --file , so the script will get the file names from the configuration file and run the pipeline on all the spreadsheets: $ gawp run ERROR Output folder gawp_demo/output conflicts with existing folder. ERROR Choose a different output name or rename/delete the existing folder. An error message! The script is warning us there is an existing folder with that name. If that folder has data you want to save, either rename the folder or edit the configuration file so it has a different output folder name. In this case we know the only file in that folder is the one we just made, and we don't care if the script overwrites it. We can tell gawp to go ahead and use this folder by adding --force to the command: $ gawp run --conf linearize.toml --file data/*.xlsx --force INFO config: added geometry INFO config: added INFO config: added INFO output directory: gawp_demo/output INFO Linearizing herm_5 INFO geometry.position_frame: 100 foci INFO geometry.measurements_frame: 17 points ... INFO writing output/linearized_herm_5.csv INFO Linearizing herm_7 INFO geometry.position_frame: 100 foci INFO geometry.measurements_frame: 9 points ... INFO writing output/linearized_herm_7.csv INFO Linearizing herm_9 INFO geometry.position_frame: 100 foci INFO geometry.measurements_frame: 10 points ... INFO writing output/linearized_herm_9.csv
